extracted.intended_audience: novelists; writers and students of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on choosing and managing novelistic methods of narration (pictorial summary vs dramatic enactment), the use and limits of the omniscient author and the first-person narrator, and how to dramatize the narrator and inner life when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picture (pictorial narration) vs Drama (scenic enactment)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the method of picture-making that enables the novelist to cover his great spaces of life and quantities of experience ... As for intensity of life ... the novelist has recourse to his other arm, the one that corresponds with the single arm of the dramatist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial narration (summary, memory, consciousness) to show breadth and multitude of life that cannot be represented scene-by-scene; use drama/enactment for intensity and climactic emphasis. Recognize that every novelist will use both methods and that the craft lies in managing how story moves into and out of scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of dramatic scenes — hoard drama for important occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is the novelist’s highest light ... to use it prodigally where it is not needed is to lessen its force where it is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overuse dramatic scenes in ordinary passages; reserve scenic, enacted moments for key occasions (example: Bovary) so their force is preserved. Treat scenes as a scarce, high-value resource.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making the omniscient author conspicuous
rubrics_metrics.description: The plain pictorial method drags in the omniscient author and may make him exceedingly conspicuous ... it may contribute towards an air of ineffectiveness in a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using omniscient narration be careful not to let the author's voice intrude in ways that weaken the book's authority or produce a sense of thinness; charm/genius can hide the defect, but in ordinary work it becomes troublesome on rereading (Turgenev example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize narration — make the narrator a visible, acting presence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the consciousness of the past ... should itself become for the reader a directly perceptible fact ... that effort be given the value of a sort of drama on its own account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn the recorder into an element of the book (a narrator 'in character') so that his relation to the tale is visible and measurable. This dramatization authenticates and enhances the picture and can do double duty (authenticate and add independent interest). Thackeray's later move to a narrator-in-character is the cited model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of first-person to bound vision and give individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: The characterized 'I' is substituted for the loose and general 'I' of the author; the loss of freedom is more than repaid by the more salient effect of the picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First-person narration supplies a definite field of vision, precision, and personal colour; it tells the reader where the seer is placed and gives tone and individuality to what is seen (examples: Esmond, David Copperfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person as a compositional device to unify rambling narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: The hero gives the story an indefeasible unity by the mere act of telling it ... Autobiography — its natural right is to seem wayward and inconsequent; its charm is in the fidelity with which it follows the winding course of the writer’s thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a novel is episodic or fragmentary, first-person narration (or fictitious autobiography) can knit disparate incidents together by belonging all parts to one man; this can be a legitimate compositional advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger: first-person limited when narrator must be the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: When the man in the book is expected to make a picture of himself, a searching and elaborate portrait, then the limit of his capacity is touched and passed; the figure of the story-teller’s inner history — it is not clear that we need the intervention of anybody in this matter, and if it might be dramatized, made immediately visible, drama—
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the book’s primary subject is the narrator’s inner growth or the portrait of the narrator himself (Meredith’s Harry Richmond), relying solely on first-person report may fail: the narrator can report but cannot fully dramatize his own interior change. In such cases dramatize the narrator’s consciousness (show, don’t only tell) or choose a different method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize inner life — show rather than report
rubrics_metrics.description: What it was like to be Harry, with all that action and reaction of character and fortune proceeding within him — that is the question ... Drama we want, always drama, for the central, essential, paramount affair, whatever it is; Harry’s consciousness ought to be dramatized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For the central, transforming events and inner changes, prefer dramatic enactment (scenes, interchange, visible effects) over mere vivid autobiographical account; get 'behind' the narrator’s description so the reader can judge for themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method can correct method — combine techniques to retain advantages
rubrics_metrics.description: Method, I have said, can be imposed upon method, one kind upon another; and in analyzing the manner of certain novelists one discovers how ingeniously they will correct the weakness of one method by the force of another and retain the advantages of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible: you can apply dramatic treatment to pictorial passages, or use pictorial summary to span scope while dramatizing crucial moments. Study how successful novelists blend methods (Thackeray, Dickens, Meredith) to mitigate weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene treatment is often abused — attend to the craft of scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: On the whole, no doubt, the possibilities of the scene are greatly abused in fiction, in the daily and familiar novel. They are doubly abused; for the treatment of the scene is neglected, and yet it recurs again and again, much too often, and its value is wasted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care both to craft scenes well when you use them and to avoid excessive repetition of ill-treated scenes. Scenes should be used purposefully and with skill so their impact is preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select method according to subject — choose first person or dramatization to suit purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: David Copperfield ... was the one book in which he rejected the intrigue of action for the centre of his design ... It was a clear case for narration in person, in character ... But Meredith’s story of Harry Richmond ... the first person is used by a man who habitually avoided it ... it seemed appropriate because the story has a romantic and heroic temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match narrative method to the nature of the subject: long panoramic memory-sweeps often suit first-person chronicling (Copperfield); romantic, hero-centered portraits may require the narrator to be central (Meredith); but when inner dramatization is required prefer scenic enactment or other methods. Consider the author's intended subject (the world vs. the man) when picking viewpoint.
